sentences: The bill would amend the Asset Recycling Fund Bill 2014 to update its commencement date and make several related changes.
The amendments would replace references to the Financial Management and Accountability Act 1997 with references to the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Act 2013.
The Future Fund Board of Guardians would have 28 days from commencement to transfer money from several funds.
changes: Replace references to the FMA Act with the PGPA Act across multiple clauses.
Update the commencement clause to start on the day after Royal Assent.
Give the Future Fund Board 28 days to transfer money from the Building Australia Fund and Education Investment Fund.
Require states, territories and funding recipients to be bound by written agreements for grants.
Clarify that Commonwealth payments must be permissible under its Executive Power.
summary.affected: States, territories and funding recipients receiving payments from the Asset Recycling Fund.

The majority opposed adding [extra clauses](http://www.openaustralia.org/debate/?id=2014-06-19.29.1) into the bill. ###What were the extra clauses? The extra clauses were proposed by Labor MP [Anthony Albanese](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/grayndler/anthony_albanese) "to ensure transparency around the decisions the government makes to fund infrastructure projects" (see his [explanation](http://www.openaustralia.org/debate/?id=2014-06-19.29.1)). For example, one of the proposed clauses was that information like the cost-benefit analysis of projects given Government grants must be made public. ###Liberal rebel Liberal MP [Ken O'Dowd](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/flynn/ken_o&%2339;dowd) [crossed the floor](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/crossing-the-floor.html) to vote in favour of the idea of having a review (see [What are "Rebel Voters"?](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/help/faq#rebel)). ###Background to the bills During the [2013 election campaign](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_federal_election,_2013), Prime Minister [Tony Abbott](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/warringah/tony_abbott) said that he wanted to be known as an infrastructure prime minister (see [ABC News](http://www.abc.net.au/news/2013-08-12/party-leaders-back-on-the-campaign-trail-after-election-debate/4879458)). Bronwyn Bishop The question is twofold: that the House agree to the first proposal of agreement; the second is that the House agree to the proposal of disagreement The question is that the first proposal be agreed to. Anthony Albanese It is extraordinary that the government is moving that Senate amendments (3), (4), (7) to (11), (14), (17), (18), (22), (24) to (26), (29), (30), (35), (38) and (39) be agreed to. It is extraordinary because they are government amendments. There are 18 amendments to its own legislation. Why can't they just get it right when they write the legislation in the first place? We will be supporting the proposition of these amendments, as we will be supporting all the amendments that have been carried in the Senate and, indeed, insisting on them, because we believe this was very much flawed legislation. If you want evidence that it was flawed legislation, it is that essentially the whole parameter of this proposal, which came through the budget, was to take money that was already in the budget, in the Building Australia Fund and the Education Investment Fund, to call it something else—the Asset Recycling Fund, because that is far more polite than calling it 'privatisation encouragement'—and then to pretend that somehow this was something new. Eric Abetz I move: That the committee does not insist on its amendments to which the House of Representatives has disagreed. These two bills are an essential part of the government's plank of building the infrastructure of the 21st century. This is a plank which will allow us to develop literally tens of thousands of jobs over the next few years. This is the payment by the Commonwealth, in rough terms, of about $5,000 million, from which we ought to be able to leverage, courtesy of the states, about $33,000 million to develop the infrastructure to get the productivity enhancement projects that this country so desperately needs. Can I remind honourable senators that this bill in fact also allows the states to lease their assets, as opposed to a direct sale. We believe that it is important to have a fund such as this that can operate without the sorts of impediments that were imposed by the Senate's amendments. We believe that genuine productivity-enhancing investments are what this country needs, as opposed to the sorts of pink batts and school halls that we had in the past. In summing up, can I also indicate to the Senate that we would invite, especially senators opposite, to heed the words of their shadow spokesman Mr Marles, on 18 June 2014, when asked about this particular legislation: How could Labor stand in the way of billions, tens of billions, being spent on productive infrastructure? Mr Marles's answer was: … if the amendments don't get up, we've said we're not going to stand in the way of this bill. We would invite Labor to consider those wise words of Mr Marles. I am aware of the time constraints on the Senate. I will therefore leave my remarks at that, other than to say this is a vital part of the government's plan to get the country's economy back on track. The motion was: "That consideration of the message be made an order of the day for a later hour this day." The "message" referred to in the motion was the message from the Senate, in which the Senate insisted on the amendments it made previously. speeches.speaker: Steven Ciobo
speeches.brief: Introduced the Asset Recycling Fund Bill, which will receive an initial $5.9 billion from the Building Australia and Education Investment Funds, offer states a 15 per cent incentive payment for selling and reinvesting in infrastructure until the program closes in 2018-19, and include $350 million for the Roads to Recovery Program, managed by the Future Fund Board.

speeches.speaker: Steven Ciobo
speeches.brief: Introduced a consequential amendments bill establishing the Asset Recycling Fund by amending the COAG Reform Fund Act, the Future Fund Act, the Nation Building Funds Act and the DisabilityCare Australia Fund Act.

speeches.speaker: Anthony Albanese
speeches.brief: Argued the $5.9 billion Asset Recycling Fund is not new money but a raid on the Building Australia and Education Investment Funds, criticised the two-year, 15 per cent incentive for states to privatise assets as a flick pass of responsibility, and moved amendments requiring Infrastructure Australia assessment and parliamentary disallowance of each transaction.

speeches.speaker: Steve Irons
speeches.brief: Defended the Asset Recycling Fund, citing a 55 per cent increase in coalition infrastructure spending compared with Labor and the government's $50 billion infrastructure package, highlighted the $1.6 billion Perth Freight Link in his own electorate, and criticised Labor's record on projects like the NBN and pink batts.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Giles
speeches.brief: Criticised the $5.9 billion Asset Recycling Fund as a vehicle for privatisation with no independent Infrastructure Australia oversight, contrasted it with Labor's record raising per capita infrastructure spending from $132 to $225, and said the government would pay Victoria $1.5 billion for the East West Link despite no published business case.

speeches.speaker: Nickolas Varvaris
speeches.brief: Supported the Asset Recycling Fund Bill 2014, saying it establishes a $5 billion Asset Recycling Initiative to encourage states to sell assets and reinvest in infrastructure, and cited the WestConnex project in his Barton electorate as an $11 billion investment expected to deliver more than $20 billion in economic benefits for New South Wales.

speeches.speaker: Lisa Chesters
speeches.brief: Opposed the Asset Recycling Fund Bill 2014 as a privatisation agenda reminiscent of the Kennett government, which sold Victoria's gas and electricity utilities for $29 billion after which electricity prices rose 50 per cent, and moved amendments requiring an Infrastructure Australia cost-benefit analysis before any Commonwealth funds go to asset sales.

speeches.speaker: Michael Sukkar
speeches.brief: Noted that Victorian Labor opposition leader Daniel Andrews committed in November 2013 to sell the Port of Melbourne Corporation if elected, accusing the member for Bendigo of contradicting her own party's state policy by opposing the sale in this debate.

speeches.speaker: Michael Sukkar
speeches.brief: Defended the Asset Recycling Fund and the government's $3 billion commitment to Melbourne's East West Link stages 1 and 2, saying the project would create over 6,000 construction jobs and ease congestion for eastern suburbs commuters.

speeches.speaker: Dennis Jensen
speeches.brief: Defended the Asset Recycling Fund, highlighting the Perth Freight Link project with an estimated cost of $1.6 billion, including $925 million from the Commonwealth, and said the previous government left $195 billion in budget deficits.

speeches.speaker: Matt Thistlethwaite
speeches.brief: Criticised the Asset Recycling Fund's 15 per cent incentive payment, which public administration professor Chris Aulich described as a 'bribe', and said New South Wales energy assets return $1 billion a year to taxpayers that would be lost through privatisation.

speeches.speaker: Ewen Jones
speeches.brief: Defended the Asset Recycling Fund, highlighting $42 million for the Australian Institute of Tropical Health and Medicine, $160 million for the Townsville ring road, and $120 million for the Joint Logistics Hub in Townsville.

speeches.speaker: Pat Conroy
speeches.brief: Criticised the government for neglecting Hunter region infrastructure, noting Labor had funded and built the $1.7 billion Hunter Expressway, and said the Port of Newcastle's $1.7 billion privatisation sale returned less than $350 million to the region for projects like the Glendale Transport Interchange.

speeches.speaker: David Coleman
speeches.brief: Defended the Asset Recycling Fund and the Badgerys Creek airport decision, forecasting an extra $60 billion in GDP by 2060, and highlighted a $1.5 billion Commonwealth contribution plus a $2 billion concessional loan for the WestConnex M5 East duplication.

speeches.speaker: Shayne Neumann
speeches.brief: Condemned the Queensland LNP government's proposed $33 billion privatisation of state assets, and said Labor's $3 billion upgrade of the Ipswich Motorway between Dinmore and Darra could carry up to 100,000 vehicles a day at peak times.

speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: Argued Australia faces a significant infrastructure investment shortfall, with estimates ranging from $455 billion to $770 billion, and said the Future Fund Board of Guardians, which will manage the new $5.9 billion Asset Recycling Fund, has a proven track record growing public investments.

speeches.speaker: David Gillespie
speeches.brief: Defended the Asset Recycling Fund, highlighting $16 million in federal funding for repairs to the Bucketts Way and a further $3.5 million for Thunderbolts Way in the Lyne electorate, part of a fund expected to leverage up to $125 billion in total infrastructure investment.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Leigh
speeches.brief: Criticised the Asset Recycling Fund's 15 per cent incentive payment as resting on a shaky assumption about company tax revenue, questioned by University of Queensland economists Flavio Menezes and John Quiggin, and said states have already lost $80 billion from cuts to schools and hospitals.

speeches.speaker: Tony Smith
speeches.brief: Discussed the Asset Recycling Fund, worth $5.9 billion at commencement and offering states a 15 per cent incentive on asset sales, and accused the member for Grayndler of opposing privatisation in principle, citing his past opposition to the 1990s privatisation of the Commonwealth Bank.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: Highlighted the coalition's four election pillars, stopping the boats, repealing the carbon tax, repairing the budget and building infrastructure, citing six months without a boat arrival saving $2 billion, and disputed Labor's claim that the Moorebank Intermodal Terminal would take 3,300 trucks off the road daily, calling it a costly furphy.

speeches.speaker: Tony Zappia
speeches.brief: Criticised the Abbott government for cutting South Australia's local road supplementary funding, worth $17.8 million last year, freezing financial assistance grants worth about $920 million nationally over three years, and said South Australia would receive just $2 billion of $50 billion in forward infrastructure funding, calling the state under-funded relative to its share of roads and population.

speeches.speaker: Ed Husic
speeches.brief: Accused the Abbott government of bribing state governments to privatise assets, criticised New South Wales Premier Mike Baird's plan to sell poles and wires, noted South Australia's average electricity bill of $2335 compares with $1960 in New South Wales and Victoria after that state's privatisation, and said the Prime Minister broke a January 2013 promise of no second Sydney airport by committing to Badgerys Creek.

speeches.speaker: Graham Perrett
speeches.brief: Criticised the Asset Recycling Fund Bill as an incentive for privatisation, noting the $5.9 billion fund draws $2.4 billion from the Building Australia Fund and $3.5 billion from the Education Investment Fund.
